claim: On SWE-PRBench, no frontier model detects more than 31% of human-flagged issues from a diff alone (mean ~26% across 8 models), leaving a 20-40 percentage-point gap to human reviewers.
quote: no model detects more than 31% of human-flagged issues on the diff-only configuration ... the mean detection rate across all 8 models on config_A is approximately 26% ... the gap to human performance is approximately 20-40 percentage points

claim: Adding more context to AI reviewers degrades rather than improves performance: a 2,000-token diff-with-summary prompt beats a 2,500-token full-context prompt across all 8 models, attributed to attention dilution.
quote: a structured 2,000-token diff-with-summary prompt outperforms a 2,500-token full-context prompt enriched with execution context, import graph resolution, and test signatures across all 8 models ... attention dilution rather than poor content selection

claim: AI reviewers systematically fail on contextual and cross-file bugs: Type-2 contextual scores collapse (Sonnet 0.22->0.10) and Type-3 cross-file dependency detection is near zero, while hallucinated false-positive rates range 0.193-0.417.
quote: Type2 scores collapse at config_B across all models. Sonnet drops from 0.22 to 0.10 ... issues requiring cross-file reasoning ... Hallucination rates (False Positive Rate): Range from 0.193 to 0.417 across models

claim: On CR-Bench, a single-shot GPT-5.2 code-review agent scored 3.56% precision, 27.01% recall and 6.30% F1; a Reflexion variant raised recall to 32.76% but precision only to 5.10% (F1 8.83%), collapsing signal-to-noise from 5.11 to 1.95.
quote: Single-shot Agent (GPT-5.2): Recall: 27.01% Precision: 3.56% F1 Score: 6.30% Signal-to-Noise Ratio: 5.11 ... Reflexion Agent (GPT-5.2): Recall: 32.76% Precision: 5.10% F1 Score: 8.83% Signal-to-Noise Ratio: 1.95

claim: CR-Bench finds AI reviewers miss whole bug classes: recall of memory issues is zero for all agents, and all agents detect high-severity defects far better than low/medium ones, struggling with bugs needing external or upstream context not in the diff.
quote: Recall of memory issues is zero for all agents ... all agents demonstrate significantly higher recall for High-Severity defects compared to Low or Medium ones ... external environmental knowledge or upstream dependency context that is not fully contained within the PR diff

claim: An empirical study of 19,450 AIDev PRs found 12 of 13 code-review agents have average signal ratios below 60%, with 60.2% of closed CRA-only PRs falling in the 0-30% signal range, indicating substantial review noise.
quote: 60.2% of closed CRA-only PRs fall into the 0-30% signal range ... 12 of 13 CRAs exhibit average signal ratios below 60%, indicating substantial noise in automated review feedback

claim: PRs reviewed only by code-review agents merge at 45.20% versus 68.37% for human-only PRs (23-point gap), leading the authors to conclude agents should augment not replace human reviewers.
quote: CRA-only PRs achieve a 45.20% merge rate, 23.17 percentage points lower than human-only PRs (68.37%) ... CRAs should augment rather than replace human reviewers and that human involvement remains critical

claim: A Martian benchmark over 200,000 real PRs (Jan-Feb 2026) found the top-disclosed tool reached only 51.7% F1 (52.2% precision, 51.1% recall) while the rest of 17 tools sat near one-in-four precision.
quote: F1 Score: 51.7% Precision: 52.2% Recall: 51.1% ... the rest of the category is closer to one in four

claim: Industry false-positive rates for even the best AI code review systems sit in the 5-15% range, driven by single-line context, pattern-not-certainty inference, and missing domain knowledge.
quote: Industry benchmarks suggest that even the best AI-driven code review systems today typically achieve false-positive rates in the 5-15% range ... They may flag edge cases, misunderstand domain-specific logic, or lack context about why certain code patterns were chosen

claim: A 28-PR audit of CodeRabbit found 15% of its comments were useless/noise and 21% were nitpicking, with each inline comment firing a separate GitHub notification so teammates began auto-dismissing it within ~1.5 weeks.
quote: An audit of 28 PRs found 15% of CodeRabbit's comments were Useless/Noise and 21% were Nitpicking ... after about a week and a half, teammates were auto-dismissing CodeRabbit the way they auto-dismiss Dependabot alerts

claim: A practitioner reports AI reviewers find new things to comment on after every change, producing an 'endless loop' of refinement, and observed an AI reviewing its own suggestion then advising reverting to the original code.
quote: on every change, the AI keeps finding new things to comment on. You can end up in a sort of 'endless loop' of refinement if you're not careful
